pattern_stance_changes.reason: The only same-harness isolating comparison is the noIntent ablation, which keeps the persistent graph in both arms and removes the retrieval layer; it moves efficiency, not the solvable set, and is already credited to P24. Persistent memory itself is never removed. 'Graph memory beats in-context/plain-text memory' rests only on the Claude Code and VulnBot cross-system contrasts, which the reviewer themselves labeled 'corroborating rather than conclusive' and used to hold P36 to mixed. Applying that standard consistently, P09 is mixed, not supports.

That facts enter the graph only after a worker verifies them is a structural design property, not an isolating comparison. The only evidence that execution-verified state helps is the cross-system failure-pattern analysis (baselines show more premature-success/state-confusion), which is the same non-isolating VulnBot/Claude Code contrast the reviewer treats as mixed-grade for P36. The noIntent ablation keeps execution-verification in both arms, so it does not isolate P16. Mixed, not supports.

missed_issues: The offline intent graph is built from Pentest-R1's public training set (§5.1), and Pentest-R1 is itself one of the baselines. Even with the test-challenge blacklist, this gives Intentest a tailored domain-prior corpus that the baselines lack, an asymmetry beyond 'same model'. The noIntent ablation shows these priors move only efficiency, not solvability, so the asymmetry mainly inflates the efficiency comparison rather than the headline success numbers; the review notes same-model control but not this corpus asymmetry.

metric_mismatch on 'rounds': a round is one context-assemble/act/write-back iteration, but the four systems have very different per-round work (Intentest runs graph matching plus possibly several parallel worker calls per round). Comparing rounds across heterogeneous architectures can understate Intentest's compute; with no token or dollar reporting (§7 construct validity), the efficiency claim is not a cost claim.

The efficiency gain (33-48% fewer rounds) is prior-coverage-dependent: §6.3 says on attack surfaces without historical features the first four retrieval stages contribute nothing and the system falls back to LLM-only (Stage 5). So the measured efficiency win is partly a function of how well the author-built offline corpus covers the author-chosen test challenges, and may not transfer to novel surfaces.

Absolute task counts are tiny (~11/11/12 per difficulty bin): hard 75.0% = 9/12, so one task is ~8.3 pp. The review flags small_sample generally but not that single-task flips drive the per-bin percentages that the significance tests run on.
note: I agree with admit_with_caveats and with the review's claim grades, COI (none) and rigor (3). My blind reproducibility was 1 (no release link for Intentest or the benchmark); the review's 2 is defensible given it is built on open Cairn and the public Pentest-R1 corpus, a minor gap. The review is unusually candid (it states the DAG cannot be ablated and the no-graph attribution is cross-system). My disagreement is a consistency fix: the reviewer applied the strict 'cross-system is not isolating' rule to P36 (mixed) and P37 (introduces) but not to P09 and P16, which lean on the same cross-system/structural evidence; I downgrade both to mixed. On reflection my own blind pull toward P37 'supports' was the over-generous read the audit guidance warns against, and the reviewer's introduces is correct.
